I have been playing Far Cry 2 for more then a decade. I think it is one of the best of the series and - for it's time - truly was a unique experience. Also, there is something comforting about the atmosphere of the game.

This game is my favorite single-player first-person shooter of all time. I enjoyed Doom back in the 90s, but other than that i am not really a fan of the genre. I find the mechanics somewhat repetitive - you are forced to kill everything, everywhere, spraying bullets around like you're in some kind of direct-to-video action flick. Even acclaimed shooters like Half-Life and Bioshock come across as cartoonish and tedious to me. Counter-Strike changed everything. A game where you only get a rifle and a sidearm, where every shot matters, where a bullet to the head means instant death and spending the next few minutes learning from people far more skilled than you. After playing Counter-Strike, every first-person shooter felt like a mindless kill-fest where stealth or tactics did not matter. The good news is those things do matter in Far Cry 2.

You are still pretty much railroaded into killing everything that moves. It is an FPS, after all. But stealth always feels like a possibility. The tension before the killing ensues, the time you spend crouching motionless in elephant grass, is a highlight of the game.

The enemies in Far Cry 2 are some of the most human i have encountered. It's why killing them takes a toll - they are a lot like you. If you have been seen - if any of your enemies spot you - the whole base goes on alert. Forever. They will lay down suppressive fire in your last known position. They will wall-bang. They will establish search parties. They will freak out and start getting paranoid over the slightest noise. If you are seen - or heard - again, expect to die. One or two shots from an enemy rifle will wipe you out. But stay perfectly still, crouched in the undergrowth, and the enemy may creep past just a few meters away. And, as they widen their net, you may be able to slip through and circle round. Inevitably, shit will go south. You are spotted and clipped, then running through the jungle, sliding to obscure their line of sight, spinning round to lob a grenade or to spray and pray. Mostly, you will die. It is fucking brutal.

I know some reviewers have complained about the mechanics of this game. Respawning bases. Deteriorating weapons. Malaria. I will admit i played with Dylan's realism mod and never tried it any different, but in Dylan's mod it all makes sense. You are sick and scared and stumble into the jungle with a pea shooter. So you see an AK, grab it, but it jams in no seconds flat. You see an unguarded jeep, jump in, then get hit by an RPG half a click down the road. The game teaches you these hard lessons in the first half hour. How are you supposed to survive in Ubisoft's nightmare version of Africa? Don't pick up jury-rigged weapons. Don't jack jeeps. Wait till dusk, get your belly in the mud and proceed to your destination at a crawl. Avoid the roads, avoid the checkpoints, scout your targets and look for a headshot. Value reliability over firepower. Value cover over speed. Value your life.

The story is grim. You play an opportunistic soldier of fortune in the midst of a civil war. Almost everyone is evil and corrupt, and the vast majority attack you on sight. Even if you try to minimize casualties on an assassination or sabotage mission, something will invariably fuck up and the bodycount will rise. Or your next mission will require you to clean out a whole area anyway. Every time you hear a squeak you expect a technical to pull up and unload 50 cal into your back. Every time the sun falls on a certain pattern of leaves your trigger finger will twitch. And gosh, those hanging vines really do look like bodies sometimes, don't they? I loved Spec Ops: The Line for its simulated PTSD effects, but those were mostly scripted. Far Cry 2 plays it totally straight and your brain still goes there. Shit is fucked up, man.

So yeah. The game is punishing. It's bleak. You spend most of your time holding your breath and crouched in the dirt. Every now and then you are awed by a herd of zebra crossing the savannah at sunset, or the majesty of a tropical storm, or the slow rising moon. And then a bullet ricochets off a nearby cliff face and everything turns to shit again. A lot of games have made an impact on me due to their strong narratives. Far Cry 2 is different. The plot is thin as a potato chip, but its unforgiving sandbox houses an atmosphere thick enough to haunt me offline. Best single-player FPS since Doom? For me, yes. Hands down.

This is a fantastic game, and I personally prefer it over Far Cry 3. I was a huge fan of the original Far Cry (no, not the one on Xbox called Instincts, but the very first one on PC!). It was a flawed but fun game, with glitchy AI but beautiful levels and an open world design, where you could do a mission multiple different ways. I was worried when Far Cry 2 was announced to be in Africa and not a tropical island like the first, and that Jack Carver wouldn't be returning. I bought Far Cry 2 anyway when it released on PC, back when games didn't always come with Steam keys.

I was immediately addicted. The game is very gritty, with just about everything out to kill you. It's definitely not for casual gamers. 

Weapons start rusting and breaking after long uses, eventually exploding in your hand, damaging you and forcing you to scavenge for a weapon off the ground while enemies are shooting at you from all directions. Cars can start to break down, requiring you to quickly get out, pop the hood, and use your magical wrench to fix it all while enemies are driving down the road trying to find you. 

Bones will break. Shrapnel will stab into your thigh. Bullets will require pulling out of your arm. You'll need to heal yourself, which uniquely has your character fix himself through multiple animations of ripping out large chunks of metal from his legs, bandaging himself, etc. It all looks fantastic and gives the game, as I said earlier, a very gritty feel.

The game is flawed, just like Far Cry 1. The AI is iffy. It's hard to stealth. The story isn't delivered very well. Everyone talks like they've got to get to the last rocket off Earth. There's respawning guard outposts (though you can easily go around them, to be honest). But even with all of that said, I still think the game is much more unique and fun to play compared to Far Cry 3. I love exploring Africa, it looks gorgeous. If you ask me, I think the engine they used for FC2 (Dunia Engine) looks much better than the slightly cartoon-y style FC3 had with the Dunia Engine 2.

I'd recommend the game if you're looking for a different, less casual type of FPS. It's got an incredible amount of detail, the weapons are fun to use, there's some very cool features like weapons breaking down, the healing system, and the way AI interact with each other (enemies will try to drag their friends away after they've been hurt, for example). 

It's a very underrated game, and I hope one day we'll get another Far Cry like this. One that isn't afraid to be different and try new things.

A Good game on many accounts.

Farcry 2 is unique, fun, exciting and definately challenging. The enviroment is dynamic and beautiful, albiet sometimes locked in and small. The tactic of creating bush fires to devastate enemies has become a godsend for me.

Malaria is a topic all on it's own. Deadly, realistic and game-changing at times, it hosts a brand new, rarely implemented idea that is interesting as it is deadly.
Unfortunately, this concept is also extremely annoying and frustratingly good at stopping progress. You have to constantly backtrack to get new pills and it tends to pop up during important moments in conflict, costing you a lengthy retreat or a undeserved death.

Another issue i found was that the game feels.... crowded. You cant drive 500 yards without hitting another guard post (there are 63 in the map!) or enemy patrol. And once spotted, prepare to be tirelessly chased down and shot at until you are, injured and with a smoking engine, forced to pull over and face the threat. You can scout these posts and keep them from respawning soldiers, but it's a lengthy, time consuming process that takes away from the air of flowing gameplay and beauty otherwise found in Farcry 2.

When it comes to guns, theres a LOT. So much different weapons and tools to use, so little time. From flare guns to rocket launchers, you will never have to worry about getting bored. Gliders are fun and a great way to get from place to place. Be careful when getting off them though!

The first time I've tried to play Far Cry 2, I was kinda overwhelmed and confused by the sheer size of the world and the long stretches to go from point A to point B so I've waited to have more time at hand to dive in.

So years after, I finally managed to properly play the game and it was both satisfying and... puzzling.

Among the strong point of Far Cry 2 is - of course - the core gameplay of shooting, the rendering of an african country (especially the blinding light and sensation of heat, the heavy rains, and majesty of its landscape), and the dereliction (palpable in either Malaria, weapon degradation, and also progressive loss of humanity).

Another great feature of the game is the immersion in a civil war setting, with several factions (UFLL, APR, civils and mercenaries, weapon dealers) you're kinda "forced" to work for in order to get medication, gain weapons, reputation, money, and potentially reach your objective and leave the country. Many gray areas here where - as one would say - it is kind of difficult to distinguish good from evil, where there is only human need of survival, instinct of greed and drive to power.

All of this led to a somewhat strange place : on one hand, I enjoyed the traversal (either by foot, by car or by boat), but not so much the random encounters that acted more as disturbance in the appreciation of landscape in a disconnected, tourist way.

Like many of FPS, I played it consciously in order to "get to end", but with a growing feeling of not really knowing where I was standing in the bigger picture, questioning my own morality (if not mortality in the face of such dreadful odds) and only left with my role as a hired gun working for the highest bidder, somewhat becoming a dark character. 

For me, the most satisfying moment was the "heart of darkness", just after the prison, near the end, where everything somewhat fell in place. Evocation of Conrad's book acted as a huge relief, completely changing my perspective of the game - kinda like Bioshock ending.

So in my opinion, Far Cry 2 is a great game, not because it is an open world FPS, but because it makes you experience "the horror" and crushing power of an historical context than can lead people to commit atrocities. At some point, it's not possible to play Far Cry 2 solo storymode "for fun" - except if you embrace both the absurd and the madness.

This game is hard - Not hard in a game play way, although on Hardcore setting it is damn hard.  But hard because you aren't playing as power fantasy hero to save the day, but a desperate sick mercenary scrounging for survival in a poor as dirt African setting where its people are ugly, brutal and desperate.

There are no trigens, north koreans, frozen aliens, tibetan dictators or religious cultists - just armed thugs doing what they want through violence without a care, an experience that many people in Africa have to live through daily.  The hero isn't interested in solving any of the real issues these people have and whatever change you make is only temporary until the next warlord moves in.

If after reading that you're thinking this type of hard might appeal to you, persist through the first chapter - the Malaria is only a hassle until you get through into the open world, and then it blows wide open and you'll be on a rollercoaster ride - just don't stop to think and feel about what's going around you and how it applies to modern Africa, it might make you walk away and want to get out there and change the real world.

This game came out around the time when videogames were starting to break through in HD with awesome action movie quality. Far Cry 2 took things a step even further by implementing some innovative and immersive features. The Far Cry series really did innovate back in the day, I mean this game kicks some serious butt and it’s fun as hell to play, even 10 years after it's original release. In terms of gameplay this game could represent the pinnacle of the series because they kind of toned down some of the cooler ideas in later games.

Playing Far Cry 2 is very much like immersing yourself in an action movie. With the ability to walk over and finish off a wounded enemy who has crawled behind a fallen tree or having to take cover behind your vehicle because your gun jammed during a shoot out. The immersion is real here even in 2019, which is again 10 years after this game first came out. At a time when graphics have improved but immersive gameplay mechanics have been downgraded in a lot of AAA shooters.

The main drawback here, as with all the Far Cry games would be the repetition. Completing an excessively long campaign made up of very similar missions. Along with doing the same tasks over and over in the open world can get a little tiresome at times. However the immersive environment and fun gameplay do make up for this in my opinion. There is also fast travel available between missions which gives you the option of getting on with the campaign in a more linear style. They do also switch things up a bit fairly quickly after a few missions which helps to keep things more interesting. The fast travel is pretty cool too because like a lot of things in Far Cry 2, it’s designed for immersion over hand holding

I’ve seen people complaining online about being constantly attacked by enemies in vehicles out in the open world. I found that this can be dealt with easily by simply switching directly to your on board turret while driving. Which adds yet another cool immersive gameplay aspect to the game because you will feel more vulnerable in a civilian vehicle without a gun turret. 

The hardest difficulty mode is definitely worth trying because it really demonstrates how immersive Far Cry 2 can be. As you will be pushed to take a more strategic approach and observe what’s happening around you in the game world before taking action. However because the campaign is a bit too long and dragged out I wouldn’t recommend playing through the whole game on this difficulty level.

I would like to also mention here that Metro Exodus is heavily influenced by this game. If you play Exodus and then Far Cry 2 shortly afterwards you’ll see what I mean. I read that the developers of Metro Exodus were influenced by this game but in fact it’s pretty crazy how much design choices they took from it. I mean they were obviously heavily inspired by stuff like sleeping in safe houses. However if you actually go back and play this game you’ll see that the Metro developers took a lot more stuff that’s probably not so obvious to most gamers after 10 years have passed. As much as I love Metro Exodus it’s actually kind of bordering on plagiarism and I’m surprised that there wasn’t legal trouble over it.

In the end it’s really up to the player how much they want to get out of this game. Everything is provided here for the player to get immersed and have fun. If you take your time to appreciate this game with its emergent gameplay possibilities then you won’t really be too bothered by the repetitive elements of it’s design. Far Cry 2 is a premium experience even today in 2019 and back when it was first released it was an awesome step forward for video games in general.

The story and atmosphere are uniquely honest about the nature of war in a way the other titles of the Far Cry series simply weren't. Other entries in the series - while great in their own way - never really confronted the in-universe moral implications of killing so many people, even if they're enemy combatants. This game does; wounded enemies cry out in fear, and late-game enemies often plead for their life before you even pull the trigger simply because you've killed so many people that you've developed an almost legendary (in the monstrous sense) reputation. Enemies aren't portrayed as one-dimensional monsters, and the protagonist is repeatedly portrayed - correctly - as being no better than them morally, just better at killing and not dying. Almost everything is transactional, which is very accurate to real warfare social dynamics. It's not a perfect representation of war, sure, but it was a massive leap in the right direction for gaming - and it beats the hell out of later entries in its realism.

If you value games that are actually grounded and not just pure power fantasies with a "gritty" aesthetic, this game is for you! Even late game with the best gear and most optimized loadout, I found myself constantly hiding in bushes and tall grass whenever I even heard a vehicle in the distance because combat is almost always intensive and high-stakes. Enemy AI is surprisingly more advanced than later entries of the series, with enemy drivers attempting to ram the protagonist (usually fatal), enemy gunmen flanking as their buddies lay down suppressive fire so you can't stop them immediately, enemy snipers usually spotting you before you even see them, etc. You often have to think on your feet - running in blindly and shooting everything that moves rarely works on its own. Stealth is often more theoretically viable, but its brutal - if enemies find one body, they'll sweep the whole area and remain on high alert for quite some time - not to mention that most guns aren't even suppressed and you don't unlock the camo suit until mid-late game.

Far Cry 2 takes a noticeably harsher approach to the open-world first-person shooter than many of the games that followed it. Developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft, it drops the player into a fictional African country devastated by civil conflict, where two competing factions struggle for control while an arms dealer known as the Jackal supplies weapons that keep the violence alive. As a mercenary tasked with locating and eliminating him, the player quickly discovers that the assignment is far more complicated than simply tracking down a target.

One of the game's greatest strengths is its enormous and hostile environment. The landscape stretches across savannahs, forests, deserts, rivers, settlements, and isolated military installations, creating a convincing impression of traveling through unstable territory. Vehicles make long-distance exploration practical, but roads are filled with patrols and checkpoints that can turn an ordinary journey into a firefight. This persistent danger reinforces the idea that the player is operating in contested territory, although repeatedly fighting through repopulated checkpoints can become tiresome during longer sessions.

Combat is where Far Cry 2's systemic design becomes especially impressive. Enemy positions can be approached from multiple directions, allowing the player to use rifles from a distance, sneak closer with quieter equipment, attack aggressively with explosives, or manipulate the environment. Encounters rarely unfold exactly as planned because enemies move between positions, vehicles can unexpectedly enter the battle, weapons can malfunction, and environmental hazards can rapidly alter the situation. This unpredictability makes even relatively straightforward objectives capable of producing memorable moments.

Fire is perhaps the game's most recognizable mechanic. Flames can spread across dry vegetation and surrounding terrain, turning a carefully controlled attack into a chaotic confrontation within seconds. Starting a fire near an enemy position can force opponents from cover or block an escape route, but shifting flames can just as easily threaten the player. Combined with explosives, vehicles, destructible objects, and reactive vegetation, the fire system gives combat an organic quality that remains impressive despite the game's age.

Far Cry 2 is also unusually willing to inconvenience the player. Weapons deteriorate through use, eventually becoming unreliable and potentially jamming during combat. Picking up a worn firearm from a fallen enemy can therefore be risky, while purchasing fresh equipment provides greater reliability. Malaria adds another survival mechanic, occasionally incapacitating the protagonist and making medicine an important resource. These systems deliberately prevent the player from feeling completely comfortable. They can certainly become frustrating, but they contribute significantly to the oppressive atmosphere and distinguish the experience from more conventional power fantasies.

The campaign provides considerable freedom in deciding which assignments to pursue and how to complete them. Faction missions, side objectives, weapon-related assignments, and activities involving other mercenaries give players numerous reasons to explore. However, repetition is one of the game's most noticeable weaknesses. Many objectives eventually involve traveling considerable distances before attacking a location, eliminating someone, retrieving something, or destroying a target. The open-ended combat systems provide variety within these familiar structures, but they cannot completely eliminate the feeling of repetition.

The buddy system adds personality and consequences to the otherwise lonely mercenary experience. Other characters can become allies and occasionally offer alternative approaches to missions. They may also appear when the protagonist is in serious trouble, creating situations where the player becomes invested in keeping them alive. Combined with the morally ambiguous factions and the mysterious Jackal, these relationships reinforce a story in which there are few obvious heroes. The narrative is deliberately cynical about warfare, profiteering, and the destructive cycle created by people who continue supplying and participating in violence.

Visually, the Dunia engine helped establish a world that feels physical and reactive. Vegetation moves and burns, changing lighting conditions alter the mood of the landscape, and weather effects contribute to the atmosphere. Character animation and some environmental details inevitably reveal the game's age, yet the strong art direction prevents the presentation from feeling completely outdated. The combination of dusty roads, expansive wilderness, distant wildlife, dramatic sunsets, smoke, and spreading flames still creates a distinctive identity.

On Steam Deck, Far Cry 2 does not have the straightforward officially Verified experience associated with games specifically optimized for Valve's handheld. It should therefore be approached as a title that may require some manual configuration rather than assuming flawless compatibility. Proton selection, controller configuration, launcher behavior, resolution settings, and other adjustments may influence the experience. Once properly configured, its relatively modest hardware demands make the core game suitable for portable play, but users should expect potential compatibility quirks associated with running an older Windows title on modern handheld hardware.

Far Cry 2 remains a fascinating example of open-world design built around consequences rather than convenience. Its respawning checkpoints, extensive travel, malaria attacks, weapon degradation, and repetitive objectives can test a player's patience, yet those same uncompromising ideas help create an unusually hostile and believable atmosphere. Its dynamic fire simulation, emergent firefights, tactical freedom, morally bleak setting, and unpredictable systems give it a personality that remains difficult to replicate. Players willing to accept its deliberate roughness will find an ambitious shooter that rewards improvisation and treats survival as an important part of the adventure rather than an inconvenience to be removed.

In 2008, four years after the release of the original game, Far Cry 2 took the series to the next level with large maps and a fully open world environment. At a time when linear FPS titles were taking over the gaming scene, Far Cry 2 brought with it side quests, safe houses, a buddy system, and scoutable outposts, among other innovative systems to create a sense of realistic immersion. As far as the series' fanbase is concerned, this release is of the love it or hate it variety for a conglomeration of reasons.

At the very start of the game, players are given a choice between 9 protagonists; while their ages, ethnicities, and backgrounds vary, nothing in the game actually changes based upon who is picked. Regardless, gamers play as a mercenary who has been sent to a failed Central African state to assassinate an arms dealer known only as the Jackal. The Jackal has been providing weapons to both factions, the UFLL and the APR, thus furthering the violence in the war torn region in Africa. Upon arriving in the area, the player character comes down with a horrible case of Malaria, which causes quite a few problems in persuing the antagonist.

Let's go ahead and get this out of the way; your enjoyment of Far Cry 2 will heavily depend on what you're looking for in a game. If you're looking for another Far Cry 3 and above, you can stop reading right now and forego wasting your time. If you're looking for a game with a lot of realistic systems in place, such as weapon degradation, save states in lieu of automatic checkpoints, maps instead of HUDs, and a very sparse fast travel system, then Far Cry 2 will be right up your alley. Out of the 12 releases in the series, this game is arguably the most difficult (even on the easiest setting), most realistic, and you will almost always be engaged in either a vehicle persuit or large fire fight.

That leads us right in to what Far Cry 2 does well; total immersive realism. Weapons will degrade over time, both visually and in functionality: the more they are used, the higher the chances that they will start jamming, and they will eventually break. Guns picked up from fallen enemies are almost always already in a state of decay, and the best place to get new weapons is at the gun shop. At any given time, players can carry a special weapon, side arm, main gun, and the ever present machete; along with molotovs and grenades. There's a large arsenal to be enjoyed in each category, and while some weapons are unlocked through story progression, most of them must be unlocked by doing side quests for the shop owners. Reliability upgrades and other assets can be purchased at the shops as well. The currency of choice here are diamonds, which can either be earned through quests, or by finding the 221 caches of them scattered throughout the world.

To add to the realism, the only fast travel points that can be used are bus terminals, which will only take gamers to the four corners of the map. Since the game is broken up into two maps, the Northern and Southern districts, players must manually travel between the North and South, as the buses do not connect the two. Safe houses in this game are just that; a place to rest, stock up on supplies, and save the game. However, due to previous complaints when the game originally released, the PC version is the only one to include "anywhere" save states. There's a handful of different vehicles, including a suped-up Gocart, some military vehicles, SUVs, an ATV, and a two-door car. If a car takes too much damage, the player must get out and repair it.

There's no shortage of stuff to do in Far Cry 2. There are a total of 32 main missions, 40 side quests, 12 buddy missions, and never ending errands for the Underground, the folks that provide the Malaria medication, as well repeating hitman contracts, and a good dose of requests from the weapons vendor. All in all, full completion comes in at around 20-25 hours of playtime. Aside from being a gopher, gamers can also scout out guard posts (a total of 57) and liberate safe houses (a total of 50). However, scouting out a guard post does not mean that it's "cleared", like in subsequent Far Cry games. Enemies in this release respawn all the time, and the only true safe areas are the aforementioned safe houses.

With all of the good that Far Cry 2 showcases, the game also comes with a major dose of the bad. There are glitches galore, especially when playing on DirectX 10; most of the problems can be ironed out simply by changing to DirectX 9 instead. Otherwise, players will be faced with a game that closes every 1-2 hours due to a massive memory leak, in-game phone calls with no audio, and "jumping" NPCs. The constantly spawning enemies can also be a problem, as they'll almost always jump in vehicles to persue the main character; this results in having to stop every 30-60 seconds to take them out, and it also makes any vehicle not donning a turret completely useless. 

The irony is that what makes Far Cry 2 so realistic can also make it incredibly annoying at times. In addition to everything else, the protagonist is battling Malaria, and a flare up can occur at any time. Not having the appropriate medication on hand can mean imminent death. The characters and storyline are also a total write off; the dialogue is sped up to such a fast pace that it's hard to absorb any of the information, and the only character with a fleshed out background is the Jackal... but you have to find his hidden tapes, which are glitched in the PC version. There's also little to no soundtrack, so there's barely any audio stimulation for the very long drives that will generally take you across the entire map for every single mission.

Again, your enjoyment of Far Cry 2 is heavily dependant on what you're looking for in a game; it's a matter of also taking the good with the bad. The purchase is a gamble all on its own, but there's an entire community of fans still dedicated to this release. On the bright side, the controls and graphics still hold up well 10 years later, and rightfully so; there's volumetric lighting, a day and night cycle, wind and rain storms, and beautiful sunsets and sunrises. There's so much to say that it's hard to pack it all in to one Steam review, and my best advice is that if you're still on the fence about the purchase, either check out some videos or read up on the refund system.

When I first played this game, I underestimated on how addictive Far Cry 2 can be. I just cannot stop playing it and kept going on for hours.


What the game did right: 

This game is similar to its predecessor but expands the limited open world that the first Far Cry game was trying to construct on.  The environment is now far more diverse, ranging from dry savannahs to humid jungles with thick vegetation.  There is also a dynamic weather system in which fog can overtake the land or a rainstorm can appear and change the way you play.

Adding to its wide ranges of landscapes, I can argue one of the more "tactical benefits" this game boasts is its fire.  A lot of games have a blaze kept at a constant size but FC 2 offers greater realism in that part. Throw a Molotov Cocktail at a dry patch of grass and see the fire consume the grass with its voracious appetite but in a humid climate, it will inflict little damage.  

The A.I. of your enemies are no longer the same "dimwits" that got slaughtered in FC 1. If you're spotted out in the open or make too much noise near guard posts, they will come for you. They also converse with each other and try to protect themselves from the player which reflects real life. In one instance, a downed mercenary will be helped by another merc. 

Stealth has been improved. If you're careful enough, your reward is being able to silently take down one enemy after another. For the most part, their awareness is fairly balanced, unlike FC 1 in which the mercs couldn't tell if someone else was firing a loud weapon but still could see the player behind tents and bushes. Also, your choices on when to use stealth makes a big difference. For example, you can go at night where potential assailants cannot easily see you but are alert. 

A unique feature that FC 2 has is its buddies. They are in the game to help you with missions, increase your reputation by providing optional quests, or save you if your well-being has been thrashed to zero. I do enjoy interacting with them upon taking missions. 

When combining the aforementioned aspects, you can do missions with almost any mentod you want.  You can either quitely sneak past foes or go in guns blazing. It's all up to you. Exploring doesn't easily get dull and the replay value is high.



While I do favor this game, some problems are existant. 


What the game should have avoided doing wrong:

The voice acting for most of the characters is inauspicious. Most of the characters speak too fast and have a flat tone. One of your buddies' dialogue sounds like it was taken from Google translate and that makes it inauthentic. 

Over time, the side missions get repetitive. The "convoy missions" are the most subjected to this.  It gets quickly mundane to find circling rival arms vendors and blow up their trucks. The worst part is if you want to have better weapons sooner, there's no other way around this other than to proceed through the main objectives most of the time. 

The "weapon degradation system" is one that I have debated in choosing if it's interesting to keep in a game or conclude it's mostly annoying to have in a firefight. As of now, I have decided that it's a nuisance as some weapons degrade too quickly and jam at the worst times. Also, close to the end of the game, even with reliability upgrades, the game will punish you if your shots miss too much and you cannot obtain new weapons (unless you stored them).

Also, the malaria mechanism is very annoying, with no way to ever stop it, only delay it. When you're under attack by that damn disease, you can barely see well and cannot sprint away from danger. Although it doesn't last that long, it may cost some precious seconds for you to flee. 

The diamond cases in this game may somewhat excite newcomers for a while but it's painful to endure when trying to reach for some diamonds on a cliff. Although not necessary to find, it's just a distraction from what the game can truly offer. 

I did mention you can interact with your buddies, but that's very limited.  All you can do is accept 2 of their quests and after that, they will just say "hi" if you meet them regularly. 

The (re)spawning of enemy mercenaries in certain locations is downright stupid. In one case, you can take down all enemies in a base but when you leave for a certain distance and look back with a scope, the place is then refilled with enemies as if nothing has happened. The developers should have put a time limit in how fast enemies can respawn when you're sufficiently far away. 

The A.I. is good when confronting them but when they drive, it's a mess. The drivers tend to have problems in making a  U-turn and are horrible in judgement. One time, a patrol car tried to run me over but it missed and plunged into the water.

Finally, the storyline is woefully linear. Though understandable, your choices are very narrow and don't have much impact on the game. Trying to avoid providing spoilers, it's the same "bad" ending, if you decide to detonate some explosives or bribe some border guards to help out a fleeing country in need. 


Other: 

I haven't tried out multiplayer yet but I have heard that it's dead, which is sad. However, if you feel like allowing your imagination demanding to make a map with the African landscape, there is a map editor that is easy to use. Shamefully, it's quite limited and it's meant for multiplayer. 

Customizing this game is almost impossible to do, unlike most games. For those who wish to mod, they will be sadden that this is almost unachievable. Still, there are a few mods that can enhance the game (and perhaps tweak balance), like Dylan's Realism Mod. 


Conclusion:

This game is definitely worth a purchase. While it may have cons, the pros in this game will entertain you and not disappoint you for at least one playthrough. If you're bored of playing games that trap you in confined spaces, get this game and feel how open it is.

This is, in my opinion, the best installment in the Far Cry series. So let me start with the bad-
-The missions can get repetitive, especially during prolonged play.
-The music is one tier above stock music. I wish it had more nuance, more variation, or at least more than a handful of the same tracks on repeat. I turned it off, personally.
-In vanilla, the enemies can be bulletspongey- but there are mods out there to fix that issue, and they're not difficult to install.
-In vanilla, the colors can be a bit washed out. Plenty of SweetFX and other mods come in handy here, and without the desaturation, the game looks much better.
-The voice acting for everybody but the three main characters and the combatant enemies is phoned in- horrible accents,  people talking like English is their second language in real life (maybe it was intentional???) and generally just sounding monotone, rushed, and bored, like the best they could come up with for voice acting talent for the buddies was interns and script monkeys, which, knowing full well the quality of the game that preceded this entry, could have very well been the case.
-More of a personal gripe, but I wish I had a way to turn up the sounds of gunshots/explosions. I can adjust the "master" volume, but apart from that the only other option is to turn on/off the music.

With that out of the way, let's talk about the good.
-The way the game handles lighting, shadows, foliage, and fire is phenomenal, especially if you consider that this game was released back when Bush Jr. was still in office.
-The gunplay, in terms of sound and recoil apart from the sponginess, is great. I play it with mods myself, and that takes what was good and makes it absolutely perfect.
-Due to the extremely limited system for fast traveling, the player is forced to explore, by foot, boat, or automobile, a diverse, hostile, atmospheric, and at times, breathtakingly beautiful rendition of a fictional, unnamed central african country. This is how fast travel ought to be in every videogame- the problem is, you'd actually have to make the game fun to explore, which, luckily, this game excells at.
-The game is brave enough to explore at least a few of the darker topics regarding war, that being the execution of suspected political dissidents, international gun-running, and the use of PMCs between rival factions for dominance, which lends to it's immersion and worldbuilding. It's dissapointing there was no more narrative focus on such ideas, or others- it's darkness and moral ambiguity is what adds punch to the otherwise hit or miss plot. The new games are fun for their own reasons, but they're absolutely goofy and whimsical by comparison- they feel like murder playgrounds rather than life or death warzones, which, while entertaining, is dissapointing when you realize what they could have achieved if they had built on the ideas of this game instead of shirking them.

TL;DR- A handful of personal gripes aside, I love this game, and I think that, with or without mods, it is the best game in the series by far. If you're looking to buy a Far Cry game and you're new to the series, look no further- just bear in mind that this is vastly, vastly different from the rest of the series.

I've lived in Southern Africa all my life, so Far Cry 2 holds a special place in my games collection. I owned the retail version when it first released, and it provided countless hours of entertainment in my high-school years. The below are my overall impressions after playing the Steam version again.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list][*][u]Highly impressive graphics, especially for its time.[/u]
I have toured a lot of Namibia and South Africa specifically. The developers did a fantastic job conveying the look and some of the subtle feel of certain landscapes you can find in real-life. It's definitely not perfect, but it's the closest depiction of my part of the world that I've ever played, visually and audibly.
[*][u]Well optimized game engine.[/u]
At the time of release, all my friends and I had trouble trying to run this anywhere near full graphics, but that was to be expected. At the time of writing (2017), even typical office computers don't have much trouble running the game anymore. Chances are you'll be able to play with a great framerate on a mid-end or even low-end PC.
[*][u]Core gameplay to the Far Cry sequels.[/u]
If you're a fan of specifically Far Cry 3 and 4, there's lots for you to love here. It's not as polished as the later sequels, but there's enough to support the game on its own.
[*][u]Fun weapons![/u]
There are a good few weapons to mess around with. Most are unlocked the more you play the game. Each gun has a satisfying kick to it, even when the recoil isn't strong. It feels like it's doing proper damage. The explosives and grenade launchers are especially visceral, when combined with the cloud of leaves, branches and dust that goes flying after an explosion.
 [*][u]Enormous game world.[/u]
It's clear the developers made an effort to vary the look and feel of the different locations, so it rarely feels too similar when exploring over longer distances.
[*][u]Afrikaans?![/u]
I've never heard one of my home languages spoken in a game before, and I love hearing some of the NPCs rattle it off =D Jy maak seker 'n grap, ek moet weer herlaai? Ek glo dit nie!
[*][u]A comprehensive map editor![/u]
If you have friends that also play, you can build basic or  complex multiplayer maps with the included editor. This was the source of a LOT of chaotic fun with my high-school friends at the time.[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[*][u]Repetitive gameplay.[/u]
The core elements of Far Cry 3 and 4 are apparent, but feel like a hollow shell in comparison. Most missions feel almost exactly identical to the other. I personally enjoy some of the repetitive elements, as it makes for a predictable, yet relaxing thing to do in my down-time.
[*][u]Uncompelling story.[/u]
There's this interplay between two waring factions, but it proves meaningless in any practical sense.[b]EVERY NPC[/b] you meet outside of a hub-town is an enemy, so there's no point in observing which faction you happen to be attacking.
[*][u]Limited AI capabilities.[/u]
In rarer cases, NPCs accidentally kill each other, or blow themselves up when trying to blow you up. This starts happening more often when the enemy vehicles start sporting grenade launchers later in the game.
[*][u]Lack of practical STEALTH MECHANICS.[/u]
This point annoys me the most. There's a camouflage upgrade you can buy, but it's hard to gauge how effective it is. You can't go prone, so you only ever stand or crouch in the foliage. Sometimes enemies have a hard time spotting you, but randomly it's like they suddenly have telescopic infrared vision, and spot you far away in thick grass or jungle. There are only three silenced weapons in the game, and counterintuitively, the [b]pistol[/b] is the most effective due to its pin-point accuracy.
[u]Here's a neat trick:[/u] Aim at an enemy's head through your sniper rifle, then quickly switch to your silenced pistol, and shoot. You can get a headshot from like a kilometer away with your pistol. I really wish this gameplay element was more refined.
[*][u]Weapon degradation![/u]
This is also an annoying gameplay element. It would have been far more bearable if all your weapons didn't degrade so fast. Specifically, the silent dart rifle literally only fires about a dozen rounds before it corrodes and explodes. The .50 cal sniper rifle feels almost as fragile. Durability upgrades are available for all guns, but don't seem to help significantly enough.
[*][u]The "buddy" NPCs and their associated missions provide little to no reward.[/u]
One buddy can serve as "rescue-ready", saving you from a firefight that would have otherwise killed you, but they don't provide any other sort of bonus like weapons or diamonds, which are the in-game currency used to buy things. Another aspect to the game that I wish meant more.
[*][u]Small gripe:[/u]
Together with Jeep, Toyota should have also had a sponsorship with Ubisoft at the time. Personally, I see way more Toyotas in this part of the world than Jeeps. Some fourth-generation Toyota Hiluxes would fit into this gameworld perfectly.
[*][u]Small gripe:[/u]
On bolt-action rifles, the bolt handle should be on the right-hand side of the receiver D: They're all on the left in this game, and I just find it distracting :P[/list]

Despite the harsher criticism above, I still tremendously enjoy playing Far Cry 2, and can safely recommend the game. I feel it stands up well to the test of time, and proves for a fun little adventure to dive into in your spare time.

Instead  they're hiding inside huts waiting for you to give them passports in exchange for your malaria medication. The actual world is populated by respawning soliders and mercenaries and the wild life is just there so you can watch the hilarious ragdoll physics go into effect when you hit them with your car. Finding Diamond briefcases can be frustrating (and also makes no sense), increasing your "reputation" does nothing except make the enemies say different dialogue and have better weapons over time. And finally the way you heal damage by viscerally resetting broken fingers and pushing bullets out of your gaping wounds is brutal and awesome to watch at first, but reaches Monty Python levels of comedy when it is done multiple times in a single gunfight.

And yet, This game is fucking fantastic because what it does it does better than almost any other game. Its firefights are fantastic with smart A.I. that leaves you with a exhilarating sense of an adrenaline rush combined with a real sense of fear due to the fact that the enemies will do everything in its power to fuck you. Along with a fire mechanic that frankly is nothing more than a gorguous piece of artwork as you watch it spread throughout the dried grass and trees of the country-side and into the enemy base with the backdrop of an orange setting sun. 

The African environment feels so real, like you can really feel just how hot and unpleasant it must be just by looking at that beating sun in the sky and the shriveled up grass in the plains. Enemies constantly complain about the heat and there are empty plastic water bottles scattered everywhere. Furthermore, when you enter the bases of the Factions, you can almost feel the humidity and the laziness it would create as papers and garbage are thrown on the floor as its occupants are to drenched in sweat to really care. It reminds me of my apartment in the Summer. 

NPC dialogue is interesting to hear, especially in gunfights as they try to take you out and their hectic screams and grunts make them seem less like the super badass soldiers from every other shooters but simple mercenaries who are desperate to survive and leave this shit-hole country. A combination of their smart tactics and scared dialogue makes them seem like a threat that would play out similarly in a real life scenario and at times you even feel bad for them as it's clear despite their advantage in numbers, they're just as scared shitless as you are and do their hardest to look out for their fellow comrades.

In fact the sound design is fantastic all around, all the voice acting is great and the standout performance of the "villain" The Jackal, provides a small amount of social commentary as he justifies his lifestyle as an arms dealer. All of the guns sound really good and the cracklings of that fire are pure eargasm. The music of conga drums being violently beaten as combat starts really provides a minimal but effective approach that makes the firefights even more savage. Though an issue with the latter is that the congas start anytime you fire a gun and only stops when it's clear you were just fucking around with a goat or chicken. lulz.

Alot of the issues I mentioned in the first paragraph were fixed with Far Cry 3, which is also an amazing game. The world is lush and colorful and there is a lot to do other than shooting, there are soldiers that are on your side and also patrol the country side and will fight with you. There is Flora and Fauna that is actually dangerous to the player along with a hunting aspect. The Story is more developed with popular characters like Vaas, and of course, the fucking bases don't respawn. 

But Far Cry 2 still manages to remain relevant despite all of the improvements the third entry made. Simply because Far Cry 3 can't beat the 2nd game at what it does best: Gunfights and its fire mechanic. Far Cry 3 is an amazing game, but it feels very "video gamey". Far Cry 2 is less like a traditional Game and more like a simulation. But more than that it's a extremely unfair simulator with the cards very clearly stacked against you in every encounter, often with snipers and rocket launcher dudes covering all entrances to bases and a group of a dozen or more soldiers ready to flank you and kill you quickly while you're in the midst of suffering from a sudden bout of malaria. It's a game that is unapologetic in how dirty and below the belt it plays. 

Which is why the game suddenly begins to click when you, the player, begin to play like just as much of a dirty fucking bastard, if not more so. Use flamethrowers and molotov cocktails to make fires spread to bases and mow down the fleeing soldiers, throw grenades in areas where there are ammo boxes so that bullets begin exploding and hitting any enemy near enough to get sprayed. Buy an upgraded camo suit and silently one shot enemies in the head with your silenced pistol before taking your machine gun and killing the rest while they're off guard. Learn the layout of the land and use it to flank enemies, plant IED's on your jeep and then jump off it as it speeds into the base, then detonate it. Use a fucking mortar to scare the shit out of the enemies and make them scatter so you can pick them off one by one.

And my personal favorite. Give a non fatal shot to an enemy so that he is crying and crawling out in the open. His buddy, his dearest friend in the whole wide world will come out to try to hoist him up and get him to safety. And you just kill them both.

While Far Cry 3 is a very pretty game, with that whole paradise in hell motif going on. Far Cry 2's world is just as beautiful but in a more gritty and harsh way: Everything seems grimy, dusty and dirty, weapons that you pick up off of dead enemies and not from gun stores are rusty pieces of shit that break easily. The houses barely look like they can stand (a detriment to the game that you can't actually blow them up red faction style) and villages themselves look depressing with the lack of civilians and only soldiers, giving you an impression of what happened before you arrived on the scene. All the characters you interact with are greedy, evil shits that actively bring suffering upon the local populace for their own gain and their various mercenary lieutenants and your fellow buddies are more often then not, just scared people who got scammed into a war whose factions don't actually have the money to pay them and they're stuck unable to get out. It's an ugly, nihilistic game which despite its flaws ironically makes it one of the best games to come out in that decade, despite all its problems.

Welcome to my review of Far Cry 2. I hope I can help you to decide if you want to buy this game or not. I will try to show you the positive sides and negatives also.
Let's start with the fact that this FPS is one of the most immersive open world games you can find. All of your HUD is hidden and your map is in game (you have to bring it up to see where you want to go,there is no mini-map). When I said it is hidden,i meant that when you are exploring you won't see it,you will only see your health bar when you get hurt,and you will see your ammo when you are low or when you are about to reload.
The sound design is amazing, except for the voice action. They speak super fast and without emotion, its kinda hilarious but you get used to it. Other than that the sound quality is superb. From winds at night, to listening to the wild life in the distance – you get such a good feeling when you are exploring on feet.
Next the graphics – they are great for their time,but when you start the game you immidietly will see that they put a very big effort to make to world feel alive, the engine handles everything perfect – to the grass and trees to the enrupting flames when something blows up or you throw a molotov.
There are a lot of mission to do.
*Main Missions
*Buddy Missions
*Convoy
*Assassination
When you go to a weapon vendor, you have a pass a mission so more guns will be unlocked.Also your guns wear down the longer you use them.They start to jam in a middle of fight and eventually break.So you have to always resupply at the vendor to keep your equipment up to shape.
Last we will talk about buddy system and choices in the game.Your buddy is there to help you,when you go down,he comes and helps you – brings you to a save place while killing your attackers (which is cinematic).He can give an alternative way to pass a mission,and if he gets injured you can decide if you want to save him,or to leave him (or worse put a bullet in his head).
Now let's talk negatives about this game.
The biggest one is the respawning enemies.What I am talking about is,when you clear a checkpoint and leave it,and go for example 1km away to re-suply at weapon shop  and go back,they will be there again.Also if you try to skip it and just drive past it,they will shoot you down,and you have to fight them anyway.Also when you are exploring and traveling with your car,there will always be a jeep which is will come right to you and shoot you,so you have to stop kill them,and then move on (and again,again …).And when you are playing on higher difficulty is easier to just walk,because you can hide in the environment – but it takes more time to go from point A to point B.
If you want a good open world game,in which the game does not hold your hand,you are free to explore whenever you want,do the mission how you like, and choose who you spare or kill. This is the game for you.If you can look past the respawning enemies and jeeps you will have a great time ranging from 20h to 30 depending if you do all the side mission or not.
